summary: ERC-8004 moves no money and checks no identities, so most payment rules land on the rails and custodial wallet providers used next to it, not on the registry. The registry-specific issues are data protection (permanent public records), the absence of KYC or know-your-agent, and reliance on upgradeable contracts (one key controls them on Ethereum and Base). ERC-8226 (Draft) adds a mandate layer for agents acting on regulated tokens; it was the only such ERC a search of the ethereum/ERCs repository found on 2026-10-18. Rows are dated; check the source before relying on any of them.

rows.text: FinCEN guidance FIN-2019-G001 applies the money transmitter definition to DApps that accept and transmit value, to their owners or operators, or to both. The ERC-8004 registry contracts accept and transmit no value, so that test does not reach them. A payment provider used alongside them may be covered, depending on its role.

ERC-8004 has no KYC or know-your-agent check and screens no address, including an agentWallet. OFAC says sanctions obligations are the same for digital and fiat transactions, and that technology companies, administrators, exchangers and users of digital currencies, and other payment processors should run risk-based compliance programs that generally include sanctions list screening.

The GENIUS Act (signed 2025-07-18) regulates payment stablecoin issuers and, from 2028-07-18, bars a digital asset service provider from offering or selling a payment stablecoin to a person in the United States unless a permitted issuer issued it, subject to Treasury's limited safe harbors and an exception for qualifying foreign issuers (sections 3(b)(1), 3(c) and 18); the ERC-8004 registries issue, offer and sell none. A Federal Register search on 2026-10-18 found no final rule from a primary federal payment stablecoin regulator; Treasury's procedural interim final rule on state certifications took effect on 2026-09-30.

Regulation E and Regulation Z limit a consumer's liability for unauthorized electronic fund transfers from consumer accounts and for unauthorized credit card use; an ERC-8004 identity or reputation score does not change that allocation. A Federal Register search on 2026-10-11 found no CFPB rule on AI agents.

California's ADMT regulations (in force 2026-01-01; ADMT duties apply from 2027-01-01) cover a business that uses automated decisionmaking technology to make a significant decision about a consumer. Such decisions include providing or denying financial or lending services. Public reputation data about agents may still describe their operators.

GDPR covers any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (Article 4(1)). Feedback events, hashes and URIs cannot be deleted from the chain, which conflicts with erasure if personal data is placed there.

AI Act Article 50(1) applies from 2026-08-02: the provider of an AI system intended to interact directly with people must design it so that they are told they are dealing with an AI, unless that is obvious. The registry adds no AI Act duty of its own.

MiCA governs e-money tokens and crypto-asset service providers, including custody and transfer services for clients; the transition for existing providers ended on 2026-07-01 at the latest. Providers of non-custodial wallet software fall outside it (recital 83). The registry holds no funds; whether its ERC-721 agent tokens are crypto-assets that MiCA excludes as unique and not fungible depends on the facts (Article 2(3), recital 11).

The Transfer of Funds Regulation applies the travel rule to crypto-asset transfers when the crypto-asset service provider, or an intermediary one, of the originator or the beneficiary has its registered office in the Union. ERC-8004 defines no originator or beneficiary fields; the proofOfPayment object in its example feedback file holds fromAddress, toAddress, chainId and txHash.
PSD2 strong customer authentication applies to payment service providers; ERC-8004 identity is not an authentication factor under it.
UK GDPR, as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, keeps the right to erasure in Article 17, so the same erasure concern applies to personal data placed in permanent on-chain records.
The FCA (2026-03-25) said it will consider whether payments regulation must change for agentic AI; HM Treasury consulted from 2026-07-14 to 2026-10-06. Neither names agent registries.

The Money Laundering Regulations 2017 cover cryptoasset exchange providers and custodian wallet providers (regulation 14A) as well as credit and financial institutions. An ERC-8004 registry offers neither exchange nor custody; a payment provider used with it may be in scope, depending on its service.

PIPEDA governs personal information that organizations collect, use or disclose in the course of commercial activities, including what they write to or read from public feedback files. Individuals who handle it only for personal or domestic purposes are outside it. Collection, use and disclosure within Quebec, Alberta or British Columbia falls under provincial law instead, except at federally regulated businesses (exemption orders under section 26(2)(b)).

The Stablecoin Act in Bill C-15 received Royal Assent on 2026-03-26 but is not yet in force (Justice Laws, current to 2026-09-30). Section 97 leaves its commencement to orders of the Governor in Council. Once in force, it applies to issuers, not to identity registries.

MAS Guidelines on AI Risk Management (issued 2026-10-07, effective 2027-10-07, with Sections 5 and 6 due by 2028-10-07) cover AI agents and expect financial institutions to apply risk-based controls to third-party AI they rely on. They do not mention agent registries or reputation data.
The Personal Data Protection Act 2012 applies to personal data in public records an organization publishes.

Visa's rules govern Visa and its member institutions and yield to applicable law. Since 2025-10-18 they have required an Agentic Payment Provider to enroll in Visa Intelligent Commerce and register with Visa, directly or via an Agentic Payment Enabler (4.1.24.2). Within Visa's system, they make the cardholder responsible for the provider's actions in an Agentic Transaction as if the cardholder had initiated it. The rules do not mention ERC-8004.

Visa calls none of its agent rules a liability shift and adds no agent-specific dispute condition or fee; its April 2026 US interchange schedule has no agentic category. It does require issuers to pay for Agentic Transactions made under a cardholder's payment instructions and not to block them wholesale. From 2026-10-24 it also accepts an Agentic Payment Provider's login ID among the evidence that can defeat a card-absent fraud dispute. Worldpay (2026-07-30) says no liability shift exists yet for agentic transactions.

Mastercard's developer guidance says only registered agents can transact. The 2026-06-02 Mastercard Rules add no agent-specific liability rule. They require pass-through wallet operators and checkout facilitators in Agent Pay to follow the Mastercard Agent Pay Program Standards. A web search on 2026-10-19 found no public copy of those standards. Neither the rules nor Mastercard's developer toolkit mentions ERC-8004.
